newsitem.title: USA: HFCS seen overtaking sugar in U.S. in eight years.
newsitem.headline: HFCS seen overtaking sugar in U.S. in eight years.

text.p: Consumption of High Fructose Corn Syrup in the United States is expected to continue to expand more rapidly than rival sugar and overtake it as the country's leading sweetener in about eight years' time, a government economist said on Tuesday.

Robert Barry, an agricultural economist for the U.S. Department of Agriculture, said annual growth in sugar consumption would slow to about 1.4 percent from 1996 to 2003 from about two percent during the preceding decade, in part because of continued substitution.
HFCS currently represents about 47 percent of the combined sugar and HFCS consumption in the United States, rising from about 42 percent a decade ago.
Consumption in fiscal 1997 of HFCS is forecast to rise 4.7 percent to 8.36 million short tons, he said.

Barry noted that HFCS production capacity had grown dramatically, with some of the increase due to anticipation of larger exports to Mexico. Trade since 1994 has, however, been disrupted by the devaluation of the Mexican peso and the recent economic contraction.
He said some leading Mexican soft drink manufacturers had links to sugar cane production operations and so it may be difficult for HFCS to make headway in some areas.
"It appears that the major Mexican soft drink bottlers are adopting a "go-slow" approach to switching to HFCS, but smaller brands seem to be moving more quickly," he said.
Barry also noted media reports that Mexican sugar producers were preparing an anti-dumping petition against U.S. HFCS.
"No official anti-dumping investigation has begun," he said.
U.S. exports of HFCS to Mexico in fiscal 1996 rose to 78,000 tonnes, dry basis, from 50,000 tonnes a year earlier and only 9,000 tonnes in 1991, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.
The United States is the leading consumer of HFCS, accounting for about 75 percent of the world total.
